newsitem.title: USA: Dollar falls as chances of rate hike fade, pound gains.
newsitem.headline: Dollar falls as chances of rate hike fade, pound gains.

text.p: The dollar fell against most major currencies on Thursday as hopes for an increase in U.S. interest rates faded and traders locked in profits ahead of the long Independence Day weekend.
The dollar's losses were most pronounced against the pound, which rose sharply for a second consecutive day in anticipation of higher British rates.
Expectations of higher U.S. rates dwindled after the U.S. Labour Department's report on June employment showed an uptick in the U.S. unemployment rate to 5.0 percent from 4.8 percent in May.

The data appeared to validate the Federal Reserve's decision to keep interest rates steady after its policy meeting on Wednesday and suggested the economy may not require another rate hike in the coming months to slow it down and avert inflation.
Higher interest rates would tend to benefit the dollar by making U.S. dollar-denominated securities, such as Treasury bonds, comparatively more attractive to international investors.

"There is a shift toward the idea that the Fed is not going to move in August or even in September and if that's the case it takes away one of the dollar's main pillars of support," said Bob Savage, chief foreign exchange dealer at Lehman Brothers.
The dollar ended at 113.82 yen, down from 114.50 on Wednesday. It settled at 1.7535 marks, just below its previous closing rate of 1.7550.

The dollar pushed to its fourth consecutive three-and-a-half year high against the mark in overseas trade, but fell back when dealers saw the rise as an opportunity to book profits ahead of the long U.S. holiday weekend.

Dollar losses against the German currency were well contained, in part due to a report showing a sharp 0.8 percent decline in German manufacturing orders for May. Broad mark weakness against the yen and the British pound also helped keep dollar losses against the mark to a minimum.
The pound rose to its highest level against the mark in almost six years and surged to a high of $1.6929, its top level since early January, before settling at $1.6915, up from $1.6770 on Wednesday.

British Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown said on Thursday that he believed his budget had done what was necessary to bring fiscal and monetary policy back into balance and curb the pound's dogged gains.
But the market refused to cooperate, pushing sterling higher in anticipation of an interest rate hike from the Bank of England as early as next week.
"We saw a continuation of Wednesday's rally in sterling on the expectation of higher interest rates in Britain," said Ben Strauss, assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer.
In other trading Thursday, the dollar fell to 1.4692 Swiss francs from 1.4715 on Wednesday. The dollar also fell to Canadian $1.3736 from C$1.3760.
